title: Quinn Muir Comments On Owen Muir's Hectic Travel Plans.
subtitle: It's been a busy month.
body_html:
Dear readers, I have been on the road a bunch. I will start with a news roundup, then get to my upcoming travel!

  • I was featured on Good Morning America yesterday, and the link is here.

  • GrayMatters Health launched PRISM Imagine.

  • Radial Expands to Seven Clinics

  • Medical Device Network featured an article with your author:

When SSRIs fail: the neuromodulation pathway

Here are highlights:

Ross Law (RL): Please explain more about the rationale behind Radial.

Owen Muir (OM): Radial is bringing brain medicine to scale. When thinking about mental health, our brains control all the output that emanates from disorders such as depression, anxiety, and PTSD. Some of that is movement, some is mood, some is speech, but the common link is that these are all disorders of brain circuits.

At Radial, we treat brain circuit disorders, and as in other emergent fields such as sleep medicine, when we have a new set of tools in medicine that require sub-specialists from multiple disciplines to work together, you have a new medical discipline, and for mental health, Radial is positioned as a company that aims to bring brain medicine in a format that patients can more readily gain access to.

RL: What are the first steps in moving away from SSRIs as a first-line treatment for mental health?

OM: The first thing to look at is the data, considering whether SSRIs work, and what do we mean by work? If I told you I’m going to roll you into the OR and fix your broken leg, and it’ll work, the first time we do the operation, 30% of the time. That would mean 70% of people are going to come in for another operation, and that one will only work 5% of the time, but we’re going to keep going until either your leg snaps off or we get it right, and by the way, you’ll limp forever. This is effectively the standard of care (SoC) in psychiatry as a discipline if you only use oral medications with limited effectiveness.

And this is not even a case of trial and error because we know it’s not going to work. This situation is more like gambling in a casino where the odds are bad. For our patients, we’re playing to get them well, and to relieve their suffering, more often than not, and with fewer side effects. You shouldn’t be satisfied with things that don’t work, or alternatively, hurt people more than the illness does. And I think we’re in a similar place with the data around SSRIs.

There is more to read over on their site.

The next chance to catch up with me in person will be either at the Clinical TMS annual meeting 2026, where I have eight posters accepted (out of 88 total at the meeting). It’s June 4-6.

I’ll be headed to China with the CNS Summit Community for the Life Science Technology Forum. If you plan on being in Bejing June 11-13th—let me know.

I asked my daughter what she thought about such a trip.

A Quick Word From My Youngest Consultant

Before I head to China to speak on brain disorders and neuromodulation, I sat down with my most candid adviser — my daughter, Quinn — to get her take on the big questions in psychiatry, medical technology, and what I should say to a room full of clinicians overseas.

Owen Muir: Do you think healthcare is important?

Quinn Muir: Yes.

Owen Muir: If you had a problem — something going on in your brain — would you rather take a pill, or have your brain directly stimulated?

Quinn Muir: Brain directly.

Owen Muir: So what I mean is: if we could tickle your brain with a magnet or electricity instead of taking medicine, you’d prefer that?

Quinn Muir: Yeah.

Owen Muir: Do you think other kids would feel the same way — would they rather have a little brain tickle, or take a pill?

Quinn Muir: Either. I don’t think they want to take a pill, though. I don’t think they want that feeling.

Owen Muir: What if they had a real problem — like feeling sad, or anxious, or worried?

Quinn Muir: Oh, yeah. Then they would probably not want to take a pill.

Owen Muir: So you think anxious kids don’t want to take pills?

Quinn Muir: Mm-hmm.

Owen Muir: What about adults? Do you think they care either way?

Quinn Muir: They don’t care. They’re okay with pills and they’re okay with brain stimulation.

Owen Muir: I’m going to China. What do you think about that?

Quinn Muir: Oh, isn’t that the really, really annoying place, kind of?

Owen Muir: Well, it’s annoying to go to the consulate and get a visa. But I’ve never actually been to China before, so I can’t say whether it’s annoying or not. Did you know there are over a billion people there?

Quinn Muir: Yeah,. because everything says “Made in China.” There are a lot of things they make there.

Owen Muir: I’m going to talk about brain disorders and how they can be treated. Do you think they’ll listen to me?

Quinn Muir: Yeah, I think they’re gonna listen to you.

Owen Muir: Why?

Quinn Muir: Because you’re amazing. You make sense. Anyone can understand you. And you’re also very kind and loving.

Owen Muir: I do care a lot about people not being depressed and not having anxiety. Do you think anxiety is important?

Quinn Muir: It’s a part of life.

Owen Muir: And do you think people have too much of it? Should they have less?

Quinn Muir: I feel like... if we could make anxiety less, that’d be better for people.

Owen Muir: Do you know what depression is?

Quinn Muir: Is that when you’re, like, very depressed?

Owen Muir: You used the word in the definition. Can you say more about what it means?

Quinn Muir: (pause) ...Daddy.

Owen Muir: Have you ever been depressed?

Quinn Muir: No. Why would I?

Owen Muir: Fair enough. It’s not usually about “why would I” — it’s often about something that happens in the brain without a clear reason. Which is exactly why it matters so much to treat it well.

Owen Muir: What do you think people all over the world most want to feel?

Quinn Muir: They probably want to feel good. Like, happy.

Owen Muir: And what don’t they want to feel?

Quinn Muir: Angry. Sad. Anxious. Worried. Just... happy. They want to feel happy, joyful, loving, kind.

Owen Muir: But you also said anxiety is a part of life. So even hard feelings have a place?

Quinn Muir: Yeah. You have to go through all of that. Because that’s a part of life. Overcoming things that are hard is a good way to feel good.

Owen Muir: Is that what I should tell the people in China?

Quinn Muir: Yeah.

Owen Muir: Do you think they’ll listen?

Quinn Muir: Yeah.

Thank you, Quinn, for the vote of confidence. I’ll carry it with me to Beijing.

To our readers: Quinn wants to know if you enjoy her contributions to this newsletter. Please leave a comment below. She’s very interested in the feedback.

A Summary of Our Research to be Presented at CTMSS 2026:

Enhancing Neuroplasticity Utilizing Adjunctive D-Cycloserine During Anterior Limb of the Internal Capsule Deep Brain Stimulation for Severe Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder …A Aslam, A Lucien, MA Khan, A Goodman, O Muir

This abstract, which is also being pulled into a full paper, describes a patient who had an adequate response to accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation with the H7 coil, but a lack of durability. The patient subsequently underwent DBS for OCD, but to get to the full remission desired we used adjunctive d-cycloserine, and they were able to measure both the change in her symptoms and the change in her brain, by using the DBS electrodes to measure differences in neuroplastic effect of the drug.

One-Day and Two-Day Neuroplasticity-Enhanced TMS Regimens for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder B Marino, D Carreon, D DeSouza, K Giles, T Halene, O Muir, G Pauletti, ...

This is a publication that pools data across numbers using the Ampa-One system for rapid treatment of obsessive compulsive disorder with adjunctive DCS, the same compound we used in the paper above! The summary is that it's possible to get patient to remission of their OCD symptoms or significant improvement in one or two days of treatment using accelerated TMS to the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.

Safety and Efficacy of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Psychiatric Disorders in Pakistan A Aslam, U Zubair, O Muir

In this paper, we worked with colleagues in Pakistan to publish the first known review of transcranial magnetic stimulation in that country. They've been using TMS for a couple of years, but this is the first publish report of how it's going. The short version is TMS works in under resource countries as well as it does and well resource countries for patients who get it. I wanna thank Dr. Zubair and his team for contributing the crucial data to this publication.

One-Year Durability of the Clinical Effect of Accelerated Compared to Once-Daily Deep TMS for Depression-Long-Term Follow-Up After a Multisite Randomized Trial MS Reddy, A Mudunuru, M Bates, E Brink, M Davis, C Hanlon, L Jones, ...

This rather remarkable abstract extends on the data in the two BrainsWay SWIFT dMTS accelerated pivotal trial papers, looks at outcomes to a year. There are a lot of authors on this, but they include myself and Carlene! In summary, SWIFT dTMS is both effective and durable, with 70% less treatment days than traditional treatment.

Successful Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (dTMS) After Failure of rTMS, ECT, and Ketamine in Refractory Treatment-Resistant Depression: Real-World Case Series

A Aslam, O Muir, C Marshall, I Handoo

This abstract pools data from the inimitable Irfan Handoo and Radial to look at patients who have had successful remission of their depression, despite non-response to the combination of ECT, ketamine, in traditional rTMS in the past. It even works then! Coil geometry matters. We just don't know for whom in advance yet.

Resolution of Auditory Hallucinations in Schizoaffective Disorder Using One-Day Accelerated cTBS to the Right Temporoparietal Junction via Camera-Based Neuronavigation and D … A Lucein, A Aslam, MA Khan, C MacMillan, J Downar, O Muir

As a contribution of basic science, this is one of my favorites. We treated someone with effective disorder with a single day of cTBS—thought to be inhibitory—to the auditory cortex and her auditory hallucinations ended at the end of that single day of treatment, with just 20 stimulations across 11 total minutes of stimulation in the day. This is a single day replication of data I wrote about previously in a study using a similar approach across many days.

Rapid Remission With Durable Effects: Clinical Kinetics of Saint in Multiple Heterogeneous, Open-Label Populations TJ Ford, A Geoly, M Feyder, K Stimpson, A Maron-Katz, R Bota, ...

Along with the team at Magnus medical, we evaluated patient treated in the SAINT OLO trial, and found that in the real world, with real patients, SAINT neuromodulation works similar to lead to how it does in its clinical trials.

Replicating a Successful Five-Day Accelerated Neuronavigated TMS Treatment for Treatment-Resistant Depression Using a Scalp Measurement Approach and D-Cycloserine Augmentation …MA Khan, A Aslam, S Siddiqi, D Carreon, C MacMillan, O Muir, J Downar

This is the second publication (I also authored the first last year, and I’m still waiting for it to his the press!) replicating an expensive fMRI guided neuronavigated treatment using infrared guidance (SNT) using a camera based neuronavigation system in the single day with adjunctive DCS.

Thanks for following along, and I hope you enjoy the abstracts.
